Updated assessment with SLOOS lens:
- Policy stance: The 50 bp hike to 4.25–4.50% and guidance for “ongoing increases,” alongside continued balance-sheet runoff and money-market rate settings (IORB 4.4%, ON RRP 4.3%, primary credit 4.5%), remain clearly hawkish and restrictive.
- SLOOS signals tighter bank credit supply: Banks report broad-based tightening in standards across C&I (for large, middle-market, and small firms) and CRE (construction/land development, nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily). Standards also tightened for consumer credit (credit cards; subprime, non-QM, and jumbo mortgages), while auto loan standards were little changed. Banks are less likely to approve lower-FICO (620/680) applications and more likely to approve higher-FICO (720), indicating reduced risk appetite. Foreign banks also reported tightening in C&I.
- SLOOS shows weaker loan demand: Banks reported weaker demand for C&I loans (all firm sizes), credit cards, and auto loans, with customer needs (accounts receivable, inventory financing) cited as reasons. Demand for HELOCs was stronger, but that’s a narrow offset amid broad weakness. Residential real estate demand/standards indicate tighter and softer origination conditions.
- Macro/market implications: The combination of a restrictive Fed stance and bank tightening/softer demand reinforces a credit-driven slowdown, increasing downside risks to growth and risk assets, especially in interest-rate sensitive sectors (housing/CRE) and lower-credit consumers. This also supports disinflation over time, potentially reducing the need for an even more aggressive path later, but near-term risk sentiment is more negative than suggested by the policy statement alone.

Net: Hawkish and credibility-seeking, with SLOOS pointing to a sharper tightening in credit conditions and weaker demand that skew near-term risks more negatively than the initial read.
